docs.title: Project Context and Objectives
docs.text: Healthcare resource allocation represents a critical challenge amplified during the COVID-19 pandemic. This tutorial addresses a fundamental problem: predicting patient length of stay (LOS) to optimize hospital resource management. The HealthPlus hospital scenario provides a realistic framework for understanding how predictive modeling can directly impact operational efficiency and patient outcomes.

docs.title: Business Problem Definition
docs.text:
HealthPlus hospital faces significant revenue losses and suboptimal patient outcomes due to inefficient resource allocation. The core challenge involves predicting patient LOS during admission to enable:

  • Proactive resource planning for beds, equipment, and staff
  • Improved patient flow management throughout the hospital system
  • Cost optimization through better capacity utilization
  • Enhanced care quality via appropriate resource allocation

docs.title: Methodological Approach
docs.text:
This analysis employs a systematic regression modeling approach:

  1. Comprehensive data exploration to understand patient demographics and admission patterns
  2. Statistical correlation analysis to identify key predictive relationships
  3. Multiple regression techniques including regularization methods
  4. Feature selection optimization to balance model complexity and performance
  5. Critical performance evaluation across multiple metrics

The tutorial demonstrates how statistical modeling translates into actionable healthcare insights while maintaining analytical rigor.

docs.title: Dataset Characteristics
docs.text:
The healthcare dataset contains 500,000 patient records with 15 features capturing admission-time information. This substantial sample size enables robust statistical inference while presenting computational considerations for model training.

Key Dataset Properties: - Scale: 500,000 patients × 15 features - Completeness: No missing values detected - Scope: Admitted patients only (excludes outpatient visits) - Temporal Range: Cross-sectional admission data

docs.title: Feature Categories and Clinical Relevance
docs.text:
Patient Demographics: - Age groups and gender distribution - Previous health conditions profile

Admission Context: - Admission type (trauma, emergency, urgent) - Severity classification (extreme, moderate, minor) - Insurance status and deposit amounts

Hospital Infrastructure: - Available rooms and staff capacity - Department and ward assignments - Attending physician information

docs.title: Data Quality Assessment
docs.text:
The analysis reveals several important characteristics:

Strengths: - Complete data with no missing values - Large sample size supporting statistical power - Comprehensive feature set covering clinical and operational factors

Limitations: - Patient ID shows multiple admissions (up to 21 per patient), potentially introducing dependency - Cross-sectional design limits causal inference - No temporal tracking of patient progression during stay

Critical Insight: The maximum 21 admissions per patient suggests either chronic conditions requiring frequent hospitalization or data collection spanning multiple years. This repeat patient pattern requires careful consideration in model validation to avoid data leakage.

docs.text:

Length of Stay Distribution: - Median LOS: 9 days with range 3-51 days - Distribution shape: Right-skewed with peak at 8-9 days - Clinical interpretation: Most patients have routine stays, with few extended hospitalizations

Patient Demographics: - Age concentration: 75% of patients aged 21-50 years - Gender distribution: 74% female patients - Department focus: 68% gynecology admissions

docs.title: Correlation Analysis Results
docs.text:
A critical finding emerges from correlation analysis: continuous variables show minimal correlation with LOS, suggesting categorical variables drive prediction accuracy. This insight fundamentally shapes the modeling approach, emphasizing the importance of categorical feature engineering over numerical transformation.

Key Correlations: - Continuous variables: Near-zero correlation with LOS - Categorical relationships: Stronger associations observed - Feature independence: Minimal multicollinearity among predictors

docs.title: Ward-Level Analysis
docs.text:
Ward Performance Insights: - Ward A: Highest LOS (extreme cases, surgery patients) - Ward C: Second highest LOS (complex cases) - Wards B, D, F: Dedicated gynecology units with shorter stays

This ward-based segmentation suggests resource allocation varies significantly by patient severity, with specialized wards requiring different staffing and equipment strategies.

docs.title: Age-Related LOS Patterns
docs.text:
Notable finding: Patients aged 1-10 and 51-100 years exhibit longer stays, contrasting with the 21-50 demographic. This pattern indicates: - Pediatric complexity: Young patients require specialized care - Geriatric considerations: Older patients need extended recovery - Gynecological efficiency: Routine procedures dominate middle-age admissions

docs.title: Categorical Encoding Approach
docs.text:

Rationale: The large dataset size supports this split ratio while maintaining substantial test set size for robust evaluation. The absence of temporal ordering allows random splitting without data leakage concerns.

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Create stacked bar plots for categorical relationships

    Parameters:
    -----------
    data : DataFrame

    predictor : str
        Independent categorical variable
    target : str

    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]

    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(

        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )

    # Stacked bar visualization
    tab.plot(
        kind="bar", 
        stacked=True, 
        figsize=(count + 1, 5)
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

docs.title: Performance Metrics Framework
docs.text:
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    """
    Calculate adjusted R-squared for regression models

    Formula: 1 - ((1 - R²) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))
    where n = sample size, k = number of predictors
    """
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]  # Number of observations
    k = predictors.shape[1]  # Number of predictors
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))

def mape_score(targets, predictions):
    """
    Mean Absolute Percentage Error calculation

    Formula: mean(|actual - predicted| / |actual|) * 100
    """
    return np.mean(np.abs(targets - predictions) / targets) * 100

def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Comprehensive regression model evaluation

    Returns:
    --------
    DataFrame with RMSE, MAE, R-squared, Adjusted R-squared, MAPE
    """
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    # Core metrics calculation
    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)
    mape = mape_score(target, pred)

    # Results dataframe
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame({
        "RMSE": rmse,
        "MAE": mae,
        "R-squared": r2,
        "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
        "MAPE": mape,
    }, index=[0])

    return df_perf

Metric Implementation Details: - Adjusted R²: Penalizes model complexity, essential for feature selection - RMSE vs MAE: RMSE penalizes large errors more heavily than MAE - MAPE: Provides interpretable percentage error for business stakeholders - DataFrame output: Consistent format for model comparison

docs.text:
from scipy import stats

def prediction_confidence_interval(model, X, alpha=0.05):
    """
    Calculate prediction confidence intervals for linear regression

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : sklearn LinearRegression
        Fitted linear regression model
    X : array-like
        Feature matrix for predictions
    alpha : float
        Significance level (default 0.05 for 95% CI)

    Returns:
    --------
    tuple : (predictions, lower_bound, upper_bound)
    """
    predictions = model.predict(X)

    # Calculate residual standard error
    residuals = y_train - model.predict(x_train)
    mse = np.mean(residuals ** 2)
    se = np.sqrt(mse)

    # t-statistic for confidence interval
    t_val = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, df=len(y_train) - X.shape[1] - 1)

    # Standard error of prediction
    se_pred = se * np.sqrt(1 + np.diag(X @ np.linalg.inv(x_train.T @ x_train) @ X.T))

    # Confidence intervals
    lower_bound = predictions - t_val * se_pred
    upper_bound = predictions + t_val * se_pred

    return predictions, lower_bound, upper_bound

def robust_model_evaluation(model, X, y, cv_folds=10, random_state=42):
    """
    Comprehensive cross-validation evaluation

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : sklearn estimator
        Model to evaluate
    X : array-like
        Feature matrix
    y : array-like
        Target vector
    cv_folds : int
        Number of cross-validation folds
    random_state : int
        Random state for reproducibility

    Returns:
    --------
    dict : Cross-validation results
    """
    # Cross-validation setup
    cv = KFold(n_splits=cv_folds, shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)

    # Multiple scoring metrics
    scoring_metrics = ['r2', 'neg_mean_squared_error', 'neg_mean_absolute_error']

    cv_results = {}
    for metric in scoring_metrics:
        scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring=metric)
        cv_results[metric] = {
            'mean': scores.mean(),
            'std': scores.std(),
            'scores': scores
        }

    return cv_results

# Example usage
cv_results = robust_model_evaluation(LinearRegression(), x_train, y_train)

docs.text:
def residual_analysis(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test):
    """
    Comprehensive residual analysis for regression diagnostics

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : fitted sklearn model
    X_train, y_train : training data
    X_test, y_test : testing data

    Returns:
    --------
    dict : Residual analysis results
    """
    # Generate predictions
    train_pred = model.predict(X_train)
    test_pred = model.predict(X_test)

    # Calculate residuals
    train_residuals = y_train - train_pred
    test_residuals = y_test - test_pred

    # Residual analysis
    analysis = {
        'train_residual_mean': train_residuals.mean(),
        'test_residual_mean': test_residuals.mean(),
        'train_residual_std': train_residuals.std(),
        'test_residual_std': test_residuals.std(),
        'train_residuals': train_residuals,
        'test_residuals': test_residuals,
    }

    # Visualization
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 10))

    # Residuals vs fitted
    axes[0, 0].scatter(train_pred, train_residuals, alpha=0.5)
    axes[0, 0].axhline(y=0, color='red', linestyle='--')
    axes[0, 0].set_title('Residuals vs Fitted (Training)')
    axes[0, 0].set_xlabel('Fitted Values')
    axes[0, 0].set_ylabel('Residuals')

    # QQ plot for normality
    stats.probplot(train_residuals, dist="norm", plot=axes[0, 1])
    axes[0, 1].set_title('Normal Q-Q Plot (Training Residuals)')

    # Histogram of residuals
    axes[1, 0].hist(train_residuals, bins=50, alpha=0.7)
    axes[1, 0].set_title('Distribution of Training Residuals')
    axes[1, 0].set_xlabel('Residuals')
    axes[1, 0].set_ylabel('Frequency')

    # Residuals vs predicted (test set)
    axes[1, 1].scatter(test_pred, test_residuals, alpha=0.5, color='orange')
    axes[1, 1].axhline(y=0, color='red', linestyle='--')
    axes[1, 1].set_title('Residuals vs Fitted (Testing)')
    axes[1, 1].set_xlabel('Fitted Values')
    axes[1, 1].set_ylabel('Residuals')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    return analysis

# Example usage
residual_results = residual_analysis(model, x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test)

def create_production_pipeline(selected_features, model_params=None):
    """
    Create production-ready prediction pipeline

    Parameters:
    -----------
    selected_features : list
        Feature names selected through feature selection
    model_params : dict
        Model hyperparameters if needed

    Returns:
    --------
    Pipeline object ready for deployment
    """
    from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
    from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
    from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

    # Feature selection transformer
    feature_selector = ColumnTransformer([
        ('selected', 'passthrough', selected_features)
    ], remainder='drop')

    # Model pipeline
    if model_params is None:
        model_params = {}

    pipeline = Pipeline([
        ('feature_selection', feature_selector),
        ('regressor', LinearRegression(**model_params))
    ])

    return pipeline

# Example pipeline creation

    selected_features=list(x_train.columns[feat_cols])
)

# Fit and validate pipeline

pipeline_predictions = production_pipeline.predict(x_test)

import joblib
from datetime import datetime

def save_model_artifacts(model, feature_names, performance_metrics, model_name):
    """
    Save model and associated metadata for production deployment

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : fitted sklearn model
    feature_names : list
        Names of features used in model
    performance_metrics : dict
        Model performance on test set
    model_name : str
        Identifier for model version
    """
    timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

    # Model artifacts
    artifacts = {
        'model': model,
        'features': feature_names,
        'performance': performance_metrics,
        'timestamp': timestamp,
        'version': model_name
    }

    # Save to disk
    filename = f"hospital_los_model_{model_name}_{timestamp}.pkl"
    joblib.dump(artifacts, filename)

    print(f"Model saved as: {filename}")
    return filename

def load_model_artifacts(filename):
    """
    Load saved model artifacts

    Parameters:
    -----------
    filename : str
        Path to saved model file

    Returns:
    --------
    dict : Model artifacts
    """
    artifacts = joblib.load(filename)
    return artifacts

# Example usage
model_filename = save_model_artifacts(
    model=lin_reg_model2,
    feature_names=list(selected_features),
    performance_metrics=lin_reg_model2_test_perf.to_dict(),
    model_name="linear_8features"
)

This comprehensive code walkthrough provides complete implementation details for every aspect of the Hospital LOS prediction analysis, from data loading through production deployment considerations.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
This analysis demonstrates that admission-time data provides substantial predictive power for hospital LOS, achieving 84% variance explanation with practical clinical accuracy. The finding that simple linear regression performs comparably to complex regularization techniques suggests that the categorical nature of healthcare decisions creates naturally separable patterns amenable to linear modeling.

The 8-feature model represents the optimal balance between predictive accuracy and operational simplicity, making it the recommended approach for clinical deployment. However, the 19% prediction error rate indicates that healthcare outcomes retain inherent uncertainty that no model can fully eliminate, emphasizing the importance of robust resource management strategies that account for prediction uncertainty.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text: BigMart, a major retail chain, faces the critical challenge of predicting sales performance across its 10 stores spanning different cities. With 1559 products generating 2013 sales data, the organization needs to understand which product and store characteristics drive revenue growth.

docs.title: Strategic Importance
docs.text:
This predictive analytics project addresses three core business needs:

  1. Inventory Management: Optimize stock levels based on predicted demand patterns
  2. Store Performance: Identify factors that differentiate high-performing from underperforming outlets
  3. Product Strategy: Understand which product characteristics correlate with higher sales

docs.title: Methodology Overview
docs.text:
Our approach employs linear regression modeling with comprehensive preprocessing, feature engineering, and statistical validation. This methodology provides both predictive capability and interpretable insights for business decision-making.

Key Analytical Framework: - Univariate Analysis: Understanding individual variable distributions - Bivariate Analysis: Exploring relationships between predictors and sales - Missing Value Treatment: Pattern-based imputation strategies - Feature Engineering: Creating meaningful derived variables - Model Building: Iterative regression with assumption validation - Statistical Testing: VIF analysis and hypothesis testing for feature selection

docs.title: Expected Outcomes
docs.text:
The final model will deliver: - Quantitative Predictions: Sales forecasts for test dataset products - Interpretable Coefficients: Understanding of factor impacts on sales - Actionable Recommendations: Data-driven strategies for sales improvement

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Structure Analysis
docs.text:
The BigMart dataset contains 8,523 training observations and 5,681 test observations with 11 feature variables and 1 target variable.

Variable Categories: - Categorical Variables (5): Item_Fat_Content, Item_Type, Outlet_Size, Outlet_Location_Type, Outlet_Type - Numerical Variables (5): Item_Weight, Item_Visibility, Item_MRP, Outlet_Establishment_Year, Item_Outlet_Sales (target) - Identifier Variables (2): Item_Identifier, Outlet_Identifier (removed for modeling)

docs.title: Critical Data Quality Issues Identified
docs.text:
1. Inconsistent Categorical Encoding The Item_Fat_Content variable shows inconsistent labeling: - "Low Fat" appears as "low fat", "LF", and "Low Fat" - "Regular" appears as "reg" and "Regular"

Business Impact: This inconsistency would create artificial categories, diluting the statistical power of the fat content variable in predicting sales.

2. Missing Value Patterns - Item_Weight: 17% missing values - Outlet_Size: 28% missing values

Strategic Implication: The high percentage of missing values requires careful treatment to avoid introducing bias into sales predictions.

docs.title: Data Preprocessing Strategy
docs.text:
Categorical Standardization: Applied lambda functions to normalize Item_Fat_Content categories, ensuring consistent encoding across training and test datasets.

Identifier Removal: Eliminated Item_Identifier and Outlet_Identifier as these provide no predictive value for sales forecasting.

Missing Value Preparation: Conducted exploratory analysis to identify patterns that would inform imputation strategies rather than arbitrary mean/median replacement.

docs.title: Quality Assurance Validation
docs.text:
Post-preprocessing validation confirmed: - Consistent categorical encodings across all variables - No remaining identifier variables - Preserved data distribution characteristics - Equivalent transformations applied to both training and test datasets

Limitations: The preprocessing approach assumes that inconsistent labeling was purely data entry error rather than meaningful business distinctions. Additionally, the removal of identifier variables assumes no geographic or product-specific effects that transcend measured characteristics.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Univariate Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Categorical Variable Distributions:

The analysis revealed several important business patterns:

Item_Fat_Content Distribution: After standardization, Low Fat products significantly outnumber Regular products, suggesting either consumer preference trends or strategic product mix decisions.

Outlet_Size Hierarchy: Medium-sized outlets dominate (after imputation), followed by Small and High outlets. This distribution pattern suggests a strategic focus on medium-format retail.

Geographic Distribution: Tier 3 locations represent the largest segment, followed by Tier 2 and Tier 1. This indicates BigMart's focus on smaller cities and towns rather than metropolitan areas.

Store Format Analysis: Supermarket Type 1 dominates the outlet mix, with roughly equal representation across Types 2, 3, and Grocery Stores.

Product Category Leadership: Fruits and Vegetables constitute the largest product category, followed by Snack Foods and Household items, reflecting typical grocery shopping patterns.

docs.title: Numerical Variable Characteristics
docs.text:
Item_Weight: Exhibits approximately uniform distribution, which simplified missing value treatment strategies.

Item_Visibility: Shows right-skewed distribution, indicating some products receive disproportionately high display allocation.

Item_MRP: Demonstrates multi-modal distribution, suggesting distinct pricing tiers in BigMart's product strategy.

docs.title: Bivariate Analysis Findings
docs.text:
Temporal Sales Patterns: Analysis of Outlet_Establishment_Year vs. Item_Outlet_Sales revealed relatively constant average sales across years, with a notable sales drop in 1998. This pattern suggests: - Store age may not be a primary sales driver - External economic factors (possibly economic crisis) impacted 1998 performance - Consistent operational standards across different store vintages

Correlation Analysis Results: - Item_MRP: Moderate positive correlation with sales (strongest predictor identified) - Item_Weight: No significant correlation with sales - Item_Visibility: Weak negative correlation, suggesting potential inverse relationship

docs.title: Critical Business Insights
docs.text:
1. Price-Sales Relationship: The strong correlation between Item_MRP and sales indicates that higher-priced items generate more revenue, supporting premium product strategies.

2. Visibility Paradox: The inverse relationship between visibility and sales suggests management may be allocating premium display space to slower-moving products to boost their performance.

3. Store Format Implications: The dominance of Supermarket Type 1 in the data may indicate this format's success or simply reflect corporate expansion strategy.

docs.title: Analytical Limitations
docs.text:
• Temporal Scope: Single-year data (2013) limits ability to identify seasonal patterns or long-term trends
  • Causality Questions: Correlation analysis cannot establish whether high MRP causes high sales or reflects demand-driven pricing
  • External Factors: The 1998 sales anomaly suggests unmeasured external variables impact performance

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Pattern-Based Imputation Approach
docs.text: Rather than applying simple mean/median imputation, the analysis employed relationship-based imputation that preserves data integrity and business logic.

docs.title: Item_Weight Imputation Analysis
docs.text:
Cross-Variable Pattern Investigation: The analysis examined Item_Weight relationships across multiple categorical combinations:

Finding 1: Item_Fat_Content × Item_Type combinations showed average weights ranging from 10-14 units, with relatively consistent patterns across categories.

Finding 2: Outlet_Type × Outlet_Location_Type combinations demonstrated consistent average weights around 13 units.

Finding 3: Item_Fat_Content × Outlet_Size combinations also showed stable weight averages around 13 units.

Imputation Strategy: Based on the consistent 10-14 range across all categorical combinations, missing Item_Weight values were imputed using a uniform distribution with parameters a=10, b=14.

Rationale: This approach maintains the original uniform distribution while incorporating business logic that weight ranges should remain consistent across product categories.

docs.title: Outlet_Size Imputation Analysis
docs.text:
Pattern Recognition Process:

Step 1: Analysis of missing Outlet_Size patterns revealed that most missing values occurred in: - Supermarket Type 1 outlets - Tier 2 locations - Low Fat product categories

Step 2: Cross-tabulation analysis identified deterministic patterns: - All Grocery Stores: Small outlet size - All Supermarket Type 2 & 3: Medium outlet size - All Tier 2 locations: Small outlet size

Implementation Strategy: Applied rule-based imputation: - Grocery Store outlets → Small - Tier 2 locations → Small

docs.title: Imputation Validation
docs.text:
Distribution Preservation: Post-imputation analysis confirmed that: - Item_Weight maintained its uniform distribution characteristics - Outlet_Size distribution aligned with business logic expectations - No artificial bias was introduced into the target variable relationship

Business Logic Consistency: The imputation rules reflected logical business relationships: - Grocery stores are typically smaller format - Tier 2 cities typically house smaller stores - Weight consistency across product categories makes operational sense

docs.title: Strategic Implications
docs.text:
Inventory Management: The weight imputation strategy ensures that demand forecasting models won't be biased by missing weight data, supporting accurate inventory calculations.

Store Classification: The outlet size imputation enables proper store format analysis, crucial for understanding performance differences across store types.

docs.title: Methodological Limitations
docs.text:
Assumption Risk: The approach assumes that missing data patterns reflect the same relationships as observed data, which may not hold if missing values are systematically different.

Temporal Stability: The patterns observed in 2013 data may not persist across different time periods or market conditions.

External Validation: The imputation strategy lacks validation against external data sources or business records.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Feature Engineering Strategy
docs.text:
Outlet_Age Creation: Generated a new variable calculating store age as (2013 - Outlet_Establishment_Year), based on the hypothesis that older stores might have higher sales due to established customer relationships.

Hypothesis Testing Result: Subsequent analysis revealed that store age showed minimal relationship with sales performance, contradicting the initial business hypothesis. This finding suggests that: - Store operational quality matters more than tenure - Market saturation may offset experience advantages - BigMart's operational standards maintain consistency across store ages

docs.title: Systematic Feature Selection Process
docs.text: The modeling process employed a rigorous iterative feature elimination approach using statistical significance testing and multicollinearity analysis.

docs.title: Multicollinearity Assessment
docs.text:
Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Analysis:

Initial Assessment: Outlet_Age showed high VIF scores (>5), indicating problematic collinearity with other temporal variables.

Decision Logic: Variables with VIF > 5 were systematically removed to prevent unstable coefficient estimates.

Business Interpretation: High multicollinearity would make it impossible to isolate individual variable effects, compromising the model's interpretability for business decision-making.

docs.title: Statistical Significance Testing
docs.text:
P-Value Analysis Framework:

Applied hypothesis testing for each variable: - Null Hypothesis: Variable has no relationship with sales - Alternative Hypothesis: Variable significantly predicts sales - Significance Threshold: p < 0.05

Elimination Sequence: 1. Item_Type categories: All p-values > 0.05 (collectively removed) 2. Item_Weight: p-value = 0.724 (removed) 3. Outlet_Location_Type: Both categories p > 0.05 (removed) 4. Outlet_Size: Both categories p > 0.05 (removed) 5. Item_Visibility: p-value = 0.064 (removed)

docs.title: Final Feature Set
docs.text: Retained Variables: - Item_MRP: Strong predictor (coefficient = 1.9555) - Item_Fat_Content_Regular: Significant category effect (coefficient = 0.0158) - Outlet_Type categories: All three supermarket types significant predictors

docs.title: Feature Selection Implications
docs.text:
Model Parsimony: The final model includes only 5 variables from the original 10+ feature set, achieving strong predictive power (R² = 0.720) with minimal complexity.

Business Interpretability: The reduced feature set focuses on actionable variables: - Pricing Strategy (Item_MRP) - Product Mix (Fat Content) - Store Format (Outlet Type)

Operational Focus: The elimination of variables like Item_Weight, Visibility, and Location Type suggests these factors are either: - Not directly controllable for sales improvement - Already optimized across the BigMart network - Secondary to format and pricing strategies

docs.title: Critical Assessment
docs.text:
Selection Bias Risk: The stepwise elimination process may have removed variables that, while individually non-significant, could contribute meaningfully in combination.

Business Logic vs. Statistical Significance: Some eliminated variables (like Item_Visibility) may have practical business importance despite statistical non-significance in this dataset.

Temporal Limitations: The feature selection is based on 2013 data patterns, which may not reflect current market dynamics or consumer preferences.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 5]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Model Development Process
docs.text: The linear regression development followed a systematic assumption-driven approach, ensuring statistical validity before drawing business conclusions.

docs.title: Initial Model Performance
docs.text:
Starting Point: The initial model with all scaled features achieved R² = 0.563, indicating moderate explanatory power but significant room for improvement.

Feature Engineering Impact: After systematic feature selection, the model maintained similar R² (~0.56) with significantly fewer variables, demonstrating that removed features added minimal predictive value.

docs.title: Assumption Validation and Model Refinement
docs.text:
1. Residual Mean Assessment - Requirement: Mean of residuals ≈ 0 - Result: Achieved (residual mean ≈ 0) - Interpretation: No systematic bias in model predictions

2. Normality of Error Terms - Test Method: Histogram analysis and visual inspection - Result: Residuals approximately normally distributed - Business Implication: Confidence intervals and significance tests are reliable

3. Linearity Assessment - Initial Evaluation: Residual vs. fitted values plot showed clear pattern - Problem Identified: Non-linear relationship between predictors and target - Solution Applied: Log transformation of target variable

docs.title: Transformation Impact Analysis
docs.text:
Log Transformation Results: - R² Improvement: 0.563 → 0.720 (significant enhancement) - Linearity Achievement: Residual plots showed random distribution post-transformation - Model Interpretation: Changed from predicting raw sales to predicting log(sales)

Business Translation: The log transformation means: - Coefficients represent proportional rather than absolute changes - Model captures multiplicative rather than additive effects - More appropriate for sales data which typically shows exponential patterns

docs.title: Final Model Equation
docs.text:
Mathematical Formula: 

log(Item_Outlet_Sales) = 4.6356 + 1.9555 × Item_MRP + 0.0158 × Item_Fat_Content_Regular + 1.9550 × Outlet_Type_Supermarket_Type1 + 1.7737 × Outlet_Type_Supermarket_Type2 + 2.4837 × Outlet_Type_Supermarket_Type3

docs.title: Coefficient Interpretation
docs.text:
Item_MRP (1.9555): A one-unit increase in (scaled) MRP increases log(sales) by 1.9555 units. This represents the strongest individual predictor.

Item_Fat_Content_Regular (0.0158): Regular fat products have slightly higher log(sales) than Low Fat products (reference category).

Outlet_Type Coefficients: - Supermarket Type 3 (2.4837): Highest sales performance - Supermarket Type 1 (1.9550): Moderate performance - Supermarket Type 2 (1.7737): Lower performance - Grocery Store: Reference category (lowest performance)

docs.title: Model Performance Metrics
docs.text: Training Performance: - R-squared: 0.720 (explains 72% of sales variance) - Adjusted R-squared: High value indicates good fit accounting for variables - MSE: 0.288 (on log scale) - RMSE: 0.537 (on log scale)

docs.title: Cross-Validation Results
docs.text: 10-Fold Cross-Validation: - Mean R²: 0.718 (consistent with training) - Mean MSE: 0.290 (stable performance) - Performance Assessment: Model shows good generalization (just right fit)

docs.title: Business Strategy Implications
docs.text:
Pricing Strategy: The strong MRP coefficient suggests revenue optimization through strategic pricing rather than volume-focused discounting.

Store Format Strategy: Supermarket Type 3 format shows superior performance, suggesting expansion or conversion opportunities.

Product Mix Optimization: The minimal fat content effect suggests this is not a primary driver for sales optimization.

docs.title: Model Limitations
docs.text:
Linearity Assumption: Even after log transformation, linear regression assumes constant proportional relationships, which may not hold across all price ranges or store formats.

Feature Interactions: The model doesn't capture potential interaction effects between MRP and store format or other variable combinations.

Temporal Stability: Coefficients based on 2013 data may not reflect current market dynamics or consumer preferences.

External Factors: The model cannot account for competition, local economic conditions, or seasonal variations not captured in the dataset.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 6]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Comprehensive Assumption Testing
docs.text: Linear regression requires four critical assumptions to be valid. The analysis systematically tested and addressed each assumption.

docs.title: Mean of Residuals Validation
docs.text: Test Result: Residual mean = -1.48e-15 (essentially 0) Status: ✅ Assumption satisfied Interpretation: The model shows no systematic bias in predictions, indicating unbiased coefficient estimates.

docs.title: Normality of Error Terms
docs.text: Visual Assessment: Histogram of residuals with KDE overlay showed approximately normal distribution Statistical Implication: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are statistically reliable Business Impact: Prediction intervals for sales forecasts will be accurate

docs.title: Linearity Testing and Resolution
docs.text:
Initial Problem: Residual vs. fitted values plot revealed systematic patterns, indicating non-linear relationships

Pattern Analysis: The funnel-shaped residual pattern suggested heteroscedasticity and potential non-linearity

Solution Implementation: Applied log transformation to the target variable (Item_Outlet_Sales)

Validation Result: Post-transformation residual plots showed random scatter, confirming linearity assumption satisfaction

Performance Impact: Model R² improved from 0.563 to 0.720, representing a substantial improvement in explanatory power

docs.title: Homoscedasticity Testing
docs.text: Test Applied: Goldfeld-Quandt test for heteroscedasticity Null Hypothesis: Residuals are homoscedastic (constant variance) Test Result: p-value > 0.05 Conclusion: Failed to reject null hypothesis - residuals are homoscedastic Statistical Validation: ✅ Assumption satisfied

docs.title: Transformation Interpretation Impact
docs.text:
Model Output Change: The log transformation fundamentally changed the model's interpretation:

Original Scale: Predicting absolute sales values Log Scale: Predicting proportional changes in sales

Business Translation: - Coefficients now represent percentage impacts rather than absolute dollar impacts - More appropriate for sales data which typically exhibits multiplicative rather than additive relationships - Better captures the reality that sales impacts are often proportional to current sales levels

docs.title: Cross-Validation Robustness
docs.text:
10-Fold Cross-Validation Results: - Training R²: 0.720 - CV Mean R²: 0.718 ± 0.040 - Training MSE: 0.288 - CV Mean MSE: 0.290 ± 0.058

Overfitting Assessment: The minimal difference between training and cross-validation performance indicates the model generalizes well and is not overfitted.

Model Stability: Low standard deviations in CV metrics suggest consistent performance across different data subsets.

docs.title: Residual Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Homogeneity Validation: The random scatter in final residual plots confirms that the model appropriately captures the underlying relationship without systematic patterns.

Outlier Assessment: No extreme outliers were identified that would compromise model reliability.

Prediction Reliability: The satisfied assumptions ensure that confidence intervals for individual predictions and coefficients are statistically valid.

docs.title: Assumption Testing Limitations
docs.text:
Sample Size Considerations: While the 8,523 observations provide adequate power for assumption testing, some tests may be sensitive to the large sample size.

Transformation Trade-offs: The log transformation improved linearity but requires back-transformation for business interpretation, introducing potential prediction bias.

Assumption Interdependence: Some assumption violations can mask others; the sequential testing approach may not capture all interaction effects.

docs.title: Business Validation Implications
docs.text:
Prediction Reliability: With all assumptions satisfied, the model's sales predictions can be trusted for business planning and inventory management.

Coefficient Interpretation: The statistically valid coefficients provide reliable guidance for pricing strategies and store format decisions.

Performance Monitoring: The assumption validation framework can be reapplied as new data becomes available to ensure continued model validity.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 7]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Model Performance Summary
docs.text:
Final Model Metrics: - R-squared: 0.720 (explains 72% of sales variance) - Cross-validation R²: 0.718 ± 0.040 - Mean Squared Error: 0.288 (log scale) - Root Mean Squared Error: 0.537 (log scale)

Performance Assessment: The model demonstrates strong predictive capability with good generalization, falling into the "just right fit" category rather than overfitted or underfitted.

docs.title: 1. Pricing Strategy Optimization
docs.text:
Key Finding: Item_MRP coefficient (1.9555) represents the strongest predictor in the model.

Strategic Implication: Higher-priced items generate disproportionately higher sales revenue, supporting a premium pricing strategy over volume-based discounting.

Actionable Recommendation: Allocate premium display areas and marketing focus to higher-MRP products to maximize revenue per square foot.

docs.title: 2. Store Format Performance Hierarchy
docs.text:
Performance Ranking (based on coefficients): 1. Supermarket Type 3: 2.4837 (highest sales multiplier) 2. Supermarket Type 1: 1.9550 3. Supermarket Type 2: 1.7737 4. Grocery Store: Reference (baseline performance)

Strategic Insight: Supermarket Type 3 stores generate 1.27x higher sales than Type 1 stores and 1.40x higher than Type 2 stores.

Business Recommendation: - Prioritize Type 3 format for new store openings - Consider converting underperforming Type 2 stores to Type 3 format where feasible - Investigate operational differences between formats to identify scalable best practices

docs.title: 3. Product Mix Optimization
docs.text:
Fat Content Impact: The minimal coefficient (0.0158) for Regular vs. Low Fat products indicates this distinction has limited impact on sales.

Strategic Implication: Product fat content should not be a primary focus for sales optimization efforts.

Resource Allocation: Instead of focusing on fat content, prioritize other product characteristics like pricing, category mix, and availability.

docs.title: Model Equation Business Translation
docs.text:
Mathematical Model: 

log(Sales) = 4.6356 + 1.9555×MRP + 0.0158×Regular_Fat + Store_Format_Effects

Business Translation: - Base Sales: exp(4.6356) ≈ 103 units (baseline for Low Fat products in Grocery stores) - Price Impact: Each unit increase in scaled MRP multiplies sales by exp(1.9555) ≈ 7.1x - Format Impact: Type 3 supermarkets have exp(2.4837) ≈ 12x sales multiplier vs. grocery stores

docs.title: Prediction Reliability Assessment
docs.text:
Confidence Intervals: With satisfied statistical assumptions, the model provides reliable prediction intervals for business planning.

Accuracy Expectations: The 72% R² suggests that while the model captures major sales drivers, 28% of variance remains unexplained, indicating some inherent unpredictability in sales patterns.

Practical Application: The model is sufficiently accurate for strategic planning and inventory management but should be combined with business judgment for tactical decisions.

docs.title: 1. Temporal Limitations
docs.text:
• Single-Year Data: 2013 data may not reflect current market conditions
  • Seasonal Patterns: Unable to capture seasonal variations or trends
  • Economic Context: Model may not perform well during economic downturns or market disruptions

docs.title: 2. Model Scope Constraints
docs.text:
• Linear Relationships: Assumes constant proportional effects across all price and format ranges
  • Missing Interactions: Doesn't capture potential synergies between price and store format
  • External Factors: Cannot account for competition, local market conditions, or promotional activities

docs.title: 3. Implementation Challenges
docs.text:
• Log Scale Interpretation: Requires careful back-transformation for business communication
  • Feature Limitations: Success depends on variables not in the model (location quality, staff performance, etc.)
  • Dynamic Markets: Model coefficients may degrade over time as market conditions evolve

docs.title: Immediate Actions (0-6 months)
docs.text:
1. Premium Product Focus: Increase inventory and promotion of higher-MRP items
  2. Format Analysis: Conduct detailed operational analysis of Type 3 vs. other formats
  3. Prediction Implementation: Deploy model for inventory planning and sales forecasting

docs.title: Medium-term Strategy (6-18 months)
docs.text:
1. Format Optimization: Pilot conversion of select stores to Type 3 format
  2. Model Enhancement: Collect additional variables (competition, demographics, seasonality)
  3. Performance Monitoring: Track model accuracy and retrain as needed

docs.title: Long-term Vision (18+ months)
docs.text:
1. Market Expansion: Use insights to guide new store format and location decisions
  2. Advanced Analytics: Develop more sophisticated models incorporating external data
  3. Competitive Advantage: Leverage pricing and format insights for market differentiation

docs.text:
• Revenue Growth: Target 15-20% increase in Type 3 format stores
  • Inventory Efficiency: Reduce stockouts of high-MRP items by 25%

# Comprehensive data overview
def analyze_dataset_structure(df, dataset_name):

    """
    print(f"\n=== {dataset_name} Dataset Analysis ===")

docs.title: Categorical Variable Analysis
docs.text:
def create_categorical_plots(df, categorical_vars, figsize=(18, 10)):
    """
    Creates comprehensive categorical variable visualizations

    Parameters:
    df (DataFrame): Dataset containing categorical variables
    categorical_vars (list): List of categorical variable names
    figsize (tuple): Figure size for subplots
    """
    # Calculate subplot dimensions
    n_vars = len(categorical_vars)
    n_cols = 2
    n_rows = (n_vars + 1) // 2

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=figsize)
    fig.suptitle('Distribution of Categorical Variables', fontsize=16)

    # Flatten axes array for easier indexing
    if n_rows == 1:
        axes = [axes]
    axes_flat = [ax for row in axes for ax in (row if hasattr(row, '__iter__') else [row])]

def detect_categorical_inconsistencies(df, cat_var):
    """
    Detects and reports categorical variable inconsistencies

    Parameters:
    df (DataFrame): Dataset to analyze
    cat_var (str): Categorical variable name

    Returns:
    dict: Dictionary of inconsistencies found
    """
    values = df[cat_var].value_counts()
    print(f"\n=== {cat_var} Value Analysis ===")
    print(values)

    # Look for potential inconsistencies (case variations, abbreviations)
    unique_values = df[cat_var].unique()
    potential_issues = {}

    for val in unique_values:
        # Check for case variations
        similar_values = [v for v in unique_values if v.lower() == val.lower() and v != val]
        if similar_values:
            potential_issues[val] = similar_values

    if potential_issues:
        print(f"\nPotential inconsistencies detected:")
        for main_val, similar_vals in potential_issues.items():
            print(f"  '{main_val}' similar to: {similar_vals}")

    return potential_issues

def impute_item_weight(df, method='uniform', a=10, b=14):
    """
    Imputes missing Item_Weight values using specified method

    Parameters:
    df (DataFrame): Dataset with missing Item_Weight values
    method (str): Imputation method ('uniform', 'mean', 'median')
    a, b (float): Parameters for uniform distribution

    Returns:
    DataFrame: Dataset with imputed values
    """
    missing_indices = df[df['Item_Weight'].isnull()].index
    n_missing = len(missing_indices)

    print(f"Imputing {n_missing} missing Item_Weight values using {method} method")

    if method == 'uniform':
        # Generate random values from uniform distribution
        imputed_values = np.random.uniform(a, b, n_missing)
        print(f"Uniform distribution parameters: a={a}, b={b}")

    elif method == 'mean':
        imputed_values = [df['Item_Weight'].mean()] * n_missing

    elif method == 'median':
        imputed_values = [df['Item_Weight'].median()] * n_missing

    # Apply imputation
    df.loc[missing_indices, 'Item_Weight'] = imputed_values

    # Validation
    print(f"Imputation complete. Remaining missing values: {df['Item_Weight'].isnull().sum()}")

    # Compare distributions
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

    plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
    plt.hist(df['Item_Weight'], bins=30, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')
    plt.title('Item_Weight Distribution After Imputation')
    plt.xlabel('Item_Weight')
    plt.ylabel('Frequency')

    plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
    plt.hist(imputed_values, bins=15, alpha=0.7, color='red', edgecolor='black')
    plt.title('Distribution of Imputed Values')
    plt.xlabel('Imputed Item_Weight')
    plt.ylabel('Frequency')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    return df

def analyze_outlet_size_patterns(df):
    """
    Analyzes patterns for Outlet_Size imputation

    Parameters:
    df (DataFrame): Dataset to analyze

    Returns:
    dict: Imputation rules
    """
    # Separate complete and missing data
    complete_data = df[df['Outlet_Size'].notnull()]
    missing_data = df[df['Outlet_Size'].isnull()]

    print("=== Outlet_Size Missing Data Analysis ===")
    print(f"Missing: {len(missing_data)}, Complete: {len(complete_data)}")

    # Analyze patterns in missing data
    print("\n--- Outlet_Type distribution in missing data ---")
    print(missing_data['Outlet_Type'].value_counts())

    print("\n--- Outlet_Location_Type distribution in missing data ---")
    print(missing_data['Outlet_Location_Type'].value_counts())

    # Create cross-tabulations for complete data
    crosstabs = {}

    # Outlet_Type vs Outlet_Size
    ct_type = pd.crosstab(complete_data['Outlet_Type'], complete_data['Outlet_Size'])
    print("\n--- Outlet_Type vs Outlet_Size (Complete Data) ---")
    print(ct_type)
    crosstabs['type'] = ct_type

    # Outlet_Location_Type vs Outlet_Size  
    ct_location = pd.crosstab(complete_data['Outlet_Location_Type'], complete_data['Outlet_Size'])
    print("\n--- Outlet_Location_Type vs Outlet_Size (Complete Data) ---")
    print(ct_location)
    crosstabs['location'] = ct_location

    # Visualize patterns
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6))

    sns.heatmap(ct_type, annot=True, fmt='d', ax=axes[0])
    axes[0].set_title('Outlet_Type vs Outlet_Size')

    sns.heatmap(ct_location, annot=True, fmt='d', ax=axes[1])
    axes[1].set_title('Outlet_Location_Type vs Outlet_Size')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Derive imputation rules
    imputation_rules = {}

    # Rule 1: All Grocery Stores are Small
    grocery_small = ct_type.loc['Grocery Store', 'Small'] == ct_type.loc['Grocery Store'].sum()
    if grocery_small:
        imputation_rules['Grocery Store'] = 'Small'
        print("\nRule 1: All Grocery Stores → Small")

    # Rule 2: All Tier 2 locations are Small
    tier2_small = ct_location.loc['Tier 2', 'Small'] == ct_location.loc['Tier 2'].sum()
    if tier2_small:
        imputation_rules['Tier 2'] = 'Small'
        print("Rule 2: All Tier 2 locations → Small")

    return imputation_rules, crosstabs

def impute_outlet_size(df, imputation_rules):
    """
    Imputes Outlet_Size using derived rules

    Parameters:
    df (DataFrame): Dataset to impute
    imputation_rules (dict): Rules for imputation

    Returns:
    DataFrame: Dataset with imputed values
    """
    initial_missing = df['Outlet_Size'].isnull().sum()

    # Apply rule-based imputation
    for rule_key, size_value in imputation_rules.items():
        if rule_key == 'Grocery Store':
            mask = (df['Outlet_Size'].isnull()) & (df['Outlet_Type'] == 'Grocery Store')
            df.loc[mask, 'Outlet_Size'] = size_value
            print(f"Imputed {mask.sum()} Grocery Store outlets as {size_value}")

        elif rule_key == 'Tier 2':
            mask = (df['Outlet_Size'].isnull()) & (df['Outlet_Location_Type'] == 'Tier 2')
            df.loc[mask, 'Outlet_Size'] = size_value
            print(f"Imputed {mask.sum()} Tier 2 outlets as {size_value}")

    final_missing = df['Outlet_Size'].isnull().sum()
    print(f"Missing values reduced from {initial_missing} to {final_missing}")

    return df

# Apply Outlet_Size analysis and imputation

train_df = impute_outlet_size(train_df, imputation_rules)

def apply_feature_scaling(train_features, test_features=None, scaler_type='minmax'):
    """
    Applies feature scaling to datasets

    Parameters:
    train_features (DataFrame): Training features
    test_features (DataFrame): Test features (optional)
    scaler_type (str): Type of scaler ('minmax', 'standard')

    Returns:
    tuple: (scaled_train, scaled_test, scaler_object)
    """
    print(f"Applying {scaler_type} scaling...")

    # Initialize scaler
    if scaler_type == 'minmax':
        scaler = MinMaxScaler()
    elif scaler_type == 'standard':
        from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
        scaler = StandardScaler()

    # Fit and transform training data
    train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(train_features)
    train_scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(
        train_scaled, 
        index=train_features.index, 
        columns=train_features.columns
    )

    print(f"Training data scaled: {train_features.shape} → {train_scaled_df.shape}")

    # Transform test data if provided
    test_scaled_df = None
    if test_features is not None:
        test_scaled = scaler.transform(test_features)
        test_scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(
            test_scaled, 
            index=test_features.index, 
            columns=test_features.columns
        )
        print(f"Test data scaled: {test_features.shape} → {test_scaled_df.shape}")

    # Show scaling impact
    print("\nScaling impact on training data:")
    print(f"Original range: [{train_features.min().min():.3f}, {train_features.max().max():.3f}]")
    print(f"Scaled range: [{train_scaled_df.min().min():.3f}, {train_scaled_df.max().max():.3f}]")

    return train_scaled_df, test_scaled_df, scaler

    print(f"Adjusted R-squared: {ols_results.rsquared_adj:.4f}")
    print(f"F-statistic: {ols_results.fvalue:.4f}")

def calculate_vif_scores(features_df, threshold=5.0):
    """
    Calculates Variance Inflation Factor scores for multicollinearity detection

    Parameters:
    features_df (DataFrame): Feature matrix
    threshold (float): VIF threshold for concern

    Returns:
    pandas.Series: VIF scores for each feature
    """
    print(f"Calculating VIF scores (threshold: {threshold})")

    # Calculate VIF for each feature
    vif_scores = pd.Series(
        [variance_inflation_factor(features_df.values, i) 
         for i in range(features_df.shape[1])],
        index=features_df.columns,
        name='VIF_Score'
    )

    # Sort by VIF score
    vif_scores = vif_scores.sort_values(ascending=False)

    print(f"\nVIF Scores:")
    print(vif_scores)

    # Identify problematic features
    high_vif = vif_scores[vif_scores > threshold]
    if len(high_vif) > 0:
        print(f"\nFeatures with VIF > {threshold}:")
        print(high_vif)
    else:
        print(f"\nNo features with VIF > {threshold}")

    # Visualize VIF scores
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
    vif_scores.plot(kind='bar')
    plt.axhline(y=threshold, color='red', linestyle='--', 
                label=f'Threshold ({threshold})')
    plt.title('Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Scores')
    plt.ylabel('VIF Score')
    plt.xlabel('Features')

def iterative_feature_selection(features, target, vif_threshold=5.0, p_threshold=0.05):
    """
    Performs iterative feature selection based on VIF and p-values

    Parameters:
    features (DataFrame): Feature matrix
    target (Series): Target variable  
    vif_threshold (float): VIF threshold for multicollinearity
    p_threshold (float): P-value threshold for significance

    Returns:
    tuple: (final_features, model_results, selection_history)
    """
    print("Starting iterative feature selection...")

    current_features = features.copy()
    selection_history = []
    iteration = 0

    while True:
        iteration += 1
        print(f"\n=== Iteration {iteration} ===")
        print(f"Current features: {list(current_features.columns)}")

        # Build model
        model = sm.OLS(target, current_features)
        results = model.fit()

        # Calculate VIF scores
        vif_scores = pd.Series(
            [variance_inflation_factor(current_features.values, i) 
             for i in range(current_features.shape[1])],
            index=current_features.columns
        )

        # Get p-values
        p_values = results.pvalues

        # Record iteration
        iteration_info = {
            'iteration': iteration,
            'features': list(current_features.columns),
            'r_squared': results.rsquared,
            'adj_r_squared': results.rsquared_adj,
            'max_vif': vif_scores.max(),
            'max_p_value': p_values.max()
        }
        selection_history.append(iteration_info)

        print(f"R-squared: {results.rsquared:.4f}")
        print(f"Max VIF: {vif_scores.max():.4f}")
        print(f"Max p-value: {p_values.max():.4f}")

        # Check for high VIF
        high_vif_features = vif_scores[vif_scores > vif_threshold]
        if len(high_vif_features) > 0:
            # Remove feature with highest VIF
            feature_to_remove = high_vif_features.index[0]
            print(f"Removing {feature_to_remove} (VIF: {high_vif_features.iloc[0]:.4f})")
            current_features = current_features.drop(feature_to_remove, axis=1)
            continue

        # Check for high p-values (excluding intercept)
        high_p_features = p_values[(p_values > p_threshold) & (p_values.index != 'const')]
        if len(high_p_features) > 0:
            # Remove feature with highest p-value
            feature_to_remove = high_p_features.index[0]
            print(f"Removing {feature_to_remove} (p-value: {high_p_features.iloc[0]:.4f})")
            current_features = current_features.drop(feature_to_remove, axis=1)
            continue

        # If we reach here, all features meet criteria
        print("Feature selection complete - all criteria met")
        break

    # Final model summary
    print(f"\n=== Final Model Summary ===")
    print(f"Features retained: {list(current_features.columns)}")
    print(f"Features removed: {len(features.columns) - len(current_features.columns)}")
    print(results.summary())

    return current_features, results, selection_history

# Apply iterative feature selection
final_features, final_results, selection_history = iterative_feature_selection(
    train_features_with_const, 
    train_target
)

def comprehensive_residual_analysis(model_results, features, target):
    """
    Performs comprehensive residual analysis for regression assumptions

    Parameters:
    model_results: Fitted statsmodels results object
    features (DataFrame): Feature matrix used in model
    target (Series): Target variable

    Returns:
    dict: Analysis results and diagnostic plots
    """
    print("=== Comprehensive Residual Analysis ===")

    # Extract residuals and fitted values
    residuals = model_results.resid
    fitted_values = model_results.fittedvalues

    # Create comprehensive diagnostic plots
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 12))

    # 1. Residuals vs Fitted Values (Linearity & Homoscedasticity)
    axes[0, 0].scatter(fitted_values, residuals, alpha=0.6)
    axes[0, 0].axhline(y=0, color='red', linestyle='--')
    axes[0, 0].set_xlabel('Fitted Values')
    axes[0, 0].set_ylabel('Residuals')
    axes[0, 0].set_title('Residuals vs Fitted Values')

    # Add lowess line to detect patterns
    from scipy import stats
    try:
        from statsmodels.nonparametric.smoothers_lowess import lowess
        lowess_line = lowess(residuals, fitted_values, frac=0.3)
        axes[0, 0].plot(lowess_line[:, 0], lowess_line[:, 1], color='blue', linewidth=2)
    except:
        pass

    # 2. Normal Q-Q Plot (Normality)
    stats.probplot(residuals, dist="norm", plot=axes[0, 1])
    axes[0, 1].set_title('Normal Q-Q Plot')

    # 3. Scale-Location Plot (Homoscedasticity)
    sqrt_abs_resid = np.sqrt(np.abs(residuals))
    axes[0, 2].scatter(fitted_values, sqrt_abs_resid, alpha=0.6)
    axes[0, 2].set_xlabel('Fitted Values')
    axes[0, 2].set_ylabel('√|Residuals|')
    axes[0, 2].set_title('Scale-Location Plot')

    # 4. Histogram of Residuals (Normality)
    axes[1, 0].hist(residuals, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')

    # Overlay normal distribution
    mu, sigma = residuals.mean(), residuals.std()
    x = np.linspace(residuals.min(), residuals.max(), 100)
    normal_curve = stats.norm.pdf(x, mu, sigma)
    axes[1, 0].plot(x, normal_curve, 'r-', linewidth=2, label='Normal Distribution')
    axes[1, 0].set_xlabel('Residuals')
    axes[1, 0].set_ylabel('Density')
    axes[1, 0].set_title('Histogram of Residuals')
    axes[1, 0].legend()

    # 5. Leverage Plot (Influential Points)
    leverage = model_results.get_influence().hat_matrix_diag
    axes[1, 1].scatter(leverage, residuals, alpha=0.6)
    axes[1, 1].set_xlabel('Leverage')
    axes[1, 1].set_ylabel('Residuals')
    axes[1, 1].set_title('Leverage vs Residuals')

    # 6. Cook's Distance (Influential Points)
    cooks_d = model_results.get_influence().cooks_distance[0]
    axes[1, 2].stem(range(len(cooks_d)), cooks_d, markerfmt=',')
    axes[1, 2].set_xlabel('Observation Index')
    axes[1, 2].set_ylabel("Cook's Distance")
    axes[1, 2].set_title("Cook's Distance")

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Statistical tests
    analysis_results = {}

    # 1. Mean of residuals (should be ≈ 0)
    residual_mean = residuals.mean()
    analysis_results['residual_mean'] = residual_mean
    print(f"Mean of residuals: {residual_mean:.6e}")

    # 2. Shapiro-Wilk test for normality
    shapiro_stat, shapiro_p = stats.shapiro(residuals[:5000])  # Limit for large datasets
    analysis_results['shapiro_test'] = {'statistic': shapiro_stat, 'p_value': shapiro_p}
    print(f"Shapiro-Wilk test: statistic={shapiro_stat:.4f}, p-value={shapiro_p:.4f}")

    # 3. Durbin-Watson test for autocorrelation
    from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import durbin_watson
    dw_stat = durbin_watson(residuals)
    analysis_results['durbin_watson'] = dw_stat
    print(f"Durbin-Watson statistic: {dw_stat:.4f}")

    return analysis_results

# Apply residual analysis to current model
residual_analysis = comprehensive_residual_analysis(final_results, final_features, train_target)

def test_homoscedasticity(features, target, residuals):
    """
    Tests for homoscedasticity using multiple methods

    Parameters:
    features (DataFrame): Feature matrix
    target (Series): Target variable
    residuals (Series): Model residuals

    Returns:
    dict: Test results
    """
    print("=== Homoscedasticity Testing ===")

    test_results = {}

    # 1. Goldfeld-Quandt Test
    try:
        gq_stat, gq_p, gq_alternative = sms.het_goldfeldquandt(target, features)
        test_results['goldfeld_quandt'] = {
            'statistic': gq_stat,
            'p_value': gq_p,
            'alternative': gq_alternative
        }
        print(f"Goldfeld-Quandt Test:")
        print(f"  F-statistic: {gq_stat:.4f}")
        print(f"  p-value: {gq_p:.4f}")
        print(f"  Result: {'Homoscedastic' if gq_p > 0.05 else 'Heteroscedastic'}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Goldfeld-Quandt test failed: {e}")

    # 2. Breusch-Pagan Test
    try:
        from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan
        bp_stat, bp_p, bp_f, bp_f_p = het_breuschpagan(residuals, features)
        test_results['breusch_pagan'] = {
            'lm_statistic': bp_stat,
            'lm_p_value': bp_p,
            'f_statistic': bp_f,
            'f_p_value': bp_f_p
        }
        print(f"\nBreusch-Pagan Test:")
        print(f"  LM statistic: {bp_stat:.4f}")
        print(f"  p-value: {bp_p:.4f}")
        print(f"  Result: {'Homoscedastic' if bp_p > 0.05 else 'Heteroscedastic'}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Breusch-Pagan test failed: {e}")

    return test_results

def apply_log_transformation(target, method='natural'):
    """
    Applies logarithmic transformation to target variable

    Parameters:
    target (Series): Target variable to transform
    method (str): Type of log transformation ('natural', 'log10', 'log2')

    Returns:
    tuple: (transformed_target, transform_function, inverse_function)
    """
    print(f"Applying {method} log transformation to target variable")

    # Check for non-positive values
    if (target <= 0).any():
        print("Warning: Non-positive values detected. Adding small constant.")
        target_adj = target + 1e-6
    else:
        target_adj = target

    # Apply transformation
    if method == 'natural':
        transformed_target = np.log(target_adj)
        transform_func = np.log
        inverse_func = np.exp
    elif method == 'log10':
        transformed_target = np.log10(target_adj)
        transform_func = np.log10
        inverse_func = lambda x: 10**x
    elif method == 'log2':
        transformed_target = np.log2(target_adj)
        transform_func = np.log2
        inverse_func = lambda x: 2**x

    # Compare distributions
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

    # Original distribution
    axes[0].hist(target, bins=30, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')
    axes[0].set_title('Original Target Distribution')
    axes[0].set_xlabel('Original Values')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('Frequency')

    # Transformed distribution
    axes[1].hist(transformed_target, bins=30, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black', color='orange')
    axes[1].set_title(f'{method.title()} Log Transformed Distribution')
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Log Transformed Values')
    axes[1].set_ylabel('Frequency')

    # Q-Q plot comparison
    from scipy import stats
    stats.probplot(transformed_target, dist="norm", plot=axes[2])
    axes[2].set_title('Q-Q Plot of Transformed Target')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Print statistics
    print(f"Original target statistics:")
    print(f"  Mean: {target.mean():.4f}, Std: {target.std():.4f}")
    print(f"  Skewness: {stats.skew(target):.4f}")

    print(f"Transformed target statistics:")
    print(f"  Mean: {transformed_target.mean():.4f}, Std: {transformed_target.std():.4f}")
    print(f"  Skewness: {stats.skew(transformed_target):.4f}")

    return transformed_target, transform_func, inverse_func

def prepare_test_data(test_df, train_features, scaler, categorical_vars):
    """
    Prepares test data using same preprocessing steps as training data

    Parameters:
    test_df (DataFrame): Raw test dataset
    train_features (DataFrame): Training features for column alignment
    scaler: Fitted scaler object
    categorical_vars (list): Categorical variables for dummy encoding

    Returns:
    DataFrame: Prepared test features
    """
    print("Preparing test data for prediction...")

    # Create copy to avoid modifying original
    test_processed = test_df.copy()

    # Remove same variables as in training
    test_processed = test_processed.drop(['Outlet_Establishment_Year'], axis=1)

    # Create dummy variables
    test_processed = pd.get_dummies(test_processed, columns=categorical_vars, drop_first=True)

    # Ensure same columns as training data
    train_cols = [col for col in train_features.columns if col != 'const']

    # Add missing columns (fill with 0)
    for col in train_cols:
        if col not in test_processed.columns:
            test_processed[col] = 0
            print(f"Added missing column: {col}")

    # Remove extra columns
    extra_cols = [col for col in test_processed.columns if col not in train_cols]
    if extra_cols:
        test_processed = test_processed.drop(extra_cols, axis=1)
        print(f"Removed extra columns: {extra_cols}")

    # Reorder columns to match training data
    test_processed = test_processed[train_cols]

    print(f"Test data shape after preprocessing: {test_processed.shape}")
    print(f"Training features shape: {len(train_cols)}")

    # Apply scaling
    test_scaled = scaler.transform(test_processed)
    test_scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(test_scaled, columns=train_cols, index=test_processed.index)

    # Add constant term
    test_scaled_df = sm.add_constant(test_scaled_df)

    # Ensure column order matches final model features
    test_scaled_df = test_scaled_df[final_features.columns]

    print("Test data preparation complete")
    return test_scaled_df

def calculate_performance_metrics(model_results, y_true=None, y_pred=None):

    # Test metrics if provided
    if y_true is not None and y_pred is not None:
        from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score

def interpret_model_coefficients(model_results, feature_names, is_log_transformed=True):
    """
    Provides business interpretation of model coefficients

    Parameters:
    model_results: Fitted statsmodels results object
    feature_names (list): List of feature names
    is_log_transformed (bool): Whether target is log-transformed

    Returns:
    DataFrame: Coefficient interpretation table
    """
    print("=== Model Coefficient Interpretation ===")

    # Extract coefficient information
    coefficients = model_results.params
    std_errors = model_results.bse
    p_values = model_results.pvalues
    conf_intervals = model_results.conf_int()

    # Create interpretation dataframe
    interpretation_df = pd.DataFrame({
        'Coefficient': coefficients,
        'Std_Error': std_errors,
        'P_Value': p_values,
        'CI_Lower': conf_intervals[0],
        'CI_Upper': conf_intervals[1]
    })

    # Add significance indicators
    interpretation_df['Significant'] = interpretation_df['P_Value'] < 0.05
    interpretation_df['Significance_Level'] = pd.cut(
        interpretation_df['P_Value'],
        bins=[0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 1.0],
        labels=['***', '**', '*', 'ns']
    )

    if is_log_transformed:
        # For log-transformed target, coefficients represent proportional changes
        interpretation_df['Percent_Impact'] = (np.exp(interpretation_df['Coefficient']) - 1) * 100
        print("Note: Target is log-transformed. Coefficients represent proportional changes.")

    print("\nCoefficient Summary:")
    print(interpretation_df)

    # Create visualization
    significant_coeffs = interpretation_df[
        (interpretation_df['Significant']) & 
        (interpretation_df.index != 'const')
    ]

    if len(significant_coeffs) > 0:
        plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))

        # Coefficient plot with confidence intervals
        y_pos = range(len(significant_coeffs))
        coeffs = significant_coeffs['Coefficient']
        errors = significant_coeffs['Std_Error']

        plt.errorbar(coeffs, y_pos, xerr=errors, fmt='o', capsize=5, capthick=2)
        plt.axvline(x=0, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
        plt.yticks(y_pos, significant_coeffs.index)
        plt.xlabel('Coefficient Value')
        plt.title('Significant Model Coefficients with Standard Errors')
        plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

    return interpretation_df

def generate_model_equation(model_results, feature_names, is_log_transformed=True):
    """
    Generates the final model equation in mathematical format

    Parameters:
    model_results: Fitted statsmodels results object
    feature_names (list): List of feature names
    is_log_transformed (bool): Whether target is log-transformed

    Returns:
    str: Formatted model equation
    """
    coefficients = model_results.params

    # Start with target variable
    if is_log_transformed:
        equation = "log(Item_Outlet_Sales) = "
    else:
        equation = "Item_Outlet_Sales = "

    # Add intercept
    equation += f"{coefficients['const']:.4f}"

    # Add feature terms
    for feature in feature_names:
        if feature != 'const':
            coeff = coefficients[feature]
            if coeff >= 0:
                equation += f" + {coeff:.4f} × {feature}"
            else:
                equation += f" - {abs(coeff):.4f} × {feature}"

    return equation

        significant_predictors = significant_predictors.drop('const')

    # Sort by coefficient magnitude
    significant_predictors['Abs_Coefficient'] = significant_predictors['Coefficient'].abs()
    significant_predictors = significant_predictors.sort_values('Abs_Coefficient', ascending=False)

    print("Top Significant Predictors (by coefficient magnitude):")
    print(significant_predictors[['Coefficient', 'P_Value', 'Percent_Impact']].head())

    # Generate specific recommendations
    for feature, row in significant_predictors.iterrows():
        coeff = row['Coefficient']
        impact = row.get('Percent_Impact', 0)

        if 'Item_MRP' in feature:
            recommendations['pricing_strategy'].append(
                f"Item_MRP shows strongest positive impact ({coeff:.4f}). "
                f"Focus on higher-value products for maximum revenue generation."
            )

        elif 'Outlet_Type' in feature:
            if coeff > 0:
                outlet_type = feature.replace('Outlet_Type_', '')
                recommendations['store_format'].append(
                    f"{outlet_type} format shows positive sales impact ({coeff:.4f}). "
                    f"Consider expanding this store format."
                )

        elif 'Item_Fat_Content' in feature:
            if coeff > 0:
                recommendations['product_mix'].append(
                    f"Regular fat content products show higher sales. "
                    f"Optimize product mix accordingly."
                )

    # Print recommendations
    for category, recs in recommendations.items():
        if recs:
            print(f"\n{category.replace('_', ' ').title()}:")
            for i, rec in enumerate(recs, 1):
                print(f"  {i}. {rec}")

    return recommendations

# Generate final model equation and recommendations
final_equation = generate_model_equation(final_results_log, final_features.columns)
print("=== Final Model Equation ===")
print(final_equation)

business_recommendations = generate_business_recommendations(coefficient_interpretation)
